p.seg: Chapter One: Inquiry into the Way
The virtue of literature is truly great!
How could it not be coexistent with Heaven and Earth?
For black and yellow are intermingled in color,
square and round are distinguished in form,
the sun and moon overlap like jade disks,
thereby displaying the image of resplendence in the sky;
mountains and rivers gleam like brocade,
thereby arranging the form of order on the earth;
these are indeed the patterns of the Dào.
Looking up, one sees radiance emitted;
looking down, one observes potential contained.
High and low are fixed in their positions,
thus the two realms (Heaven and Earth) came into being.
Only humans participate in this,
endowed with concentrated spiritual intelligence,
and are thus called the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity).
They are the excellence of the Five Elements,
and truly the heart of Heaven and Earth.
From the heart arises speech,
from speech arises civilization,
which is the natural way.
Extending to the myriad things,
both moving and growing things possess pattern.
Dragons and phoenixes display auspiciousness with colorful patterns,
tigers and leopards exhibit elegance with bright markings;
clouds and mist are sculpted in color,
surpassing the skill of painters;
grasses and trees are adorned with blossoms,
requiring no marvelous craftsmanship of brocade artisans;
how could these be external decorations?
They are naturally so.
As for the sounds of the forest forming harmonies,
they are as attuned as the *yú* flute and *sè* zither;
the springs and rocks create rhythms as they collide,
harmonizing like the *qiú* jade and *huáng* bell.
Therefore, when form is established, pattern is complete;
when sound is uttered, literature is born.
If even insentient things
abundantly possess color,
how can beings with minds
be without pattern?
The origin of humanistic pattern
begins with the Tài Jí (Great Ultimate).
To praise silently the spirits and deities,
the *Yì* (Book of Changes) images came first.
Páo Xī (Fú Xī) drew their beginning,
Zhòng Ní (Kǒng Zǐ) elaborated on their end.
And the two positions of Qián (Heaven) and Kūn (Earth)
uniquely created the "Wén Yán" (Commentary on the Words).
The pattern of words,
is the heart of Heaven and Earth!
As for the Hé Tú (Yellow River Chart) containing the Eight Trigrams,
and the Luò Shū (Luò River Writing) encompassing the Nine Categories,
the reality of jade tablets engraved with gold,
the splendor of cinnabar script on green slips,
who is in charge of them?
It is merely divine principle.
Since bird tracks replaced knotted cords,
writing began to shine forth.
The lost deeds of Yán Hào (Yán Dì and Tài Hào)
are recorded in the *Sān Fén* (Three Tombs),
but the years and ages are distant,
and their sounds and colors are untraceable.
The literature of the Táng (Yáo) and Yú (Shùn) periods
then began to flourish brilliantly.
The sovereign led the singing,
thereby expressing the intent of poetry;
Yì and Jì presented their plans,
also establishing the style of memorials and reports.
When the Xià dynasty arose,
its achievements were lofty and its merits great,
the Nine Odes were sung exclusively,
and its meritorious virtue was all the more elaborate.
Reaching the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties,
literature surpassed substance.
Wherever the *Yǎ* (Odes) and *Sòng* (Hymns) reached,
the beautiful blossoms renewed daily.
Wén Wáng suffered anxieties,
the *Yáo Cí* (Line Statements) shone brightly,
with talismans and colors both overt and hidden,
and profound meaning firm and deep.
Further, with Gōng Dàn's (Zhōu Gōng) many talents,
he promoted their magnificent brilliance,
edited the *Shī* (Odes) and compiled the *Sòng* (Hymns),
polishing the language of all.
As for Fū Zǐ (Kǒng Zǐ) succeeding the sages,
he stood out uniquely among the former wise men,
refining the *Liù Jīng* (Six Classics) in his crucible,
surely with the sound of metal and the resonance of jade.
He sculpted the emotions and nature,
and organized phrases and words.
When the wooden-tongued bell was rung, it resonated a thousand *lǐ*;
when treasured jewels were passed on, they echoed for myriad generations.
He depicted the shining glory of Heaven and Earth,
and enlightened the ears and eyes of the people.
From the Fēng lineage,
up to the Kǒng lineage,
the profound sages created the canon,
and the uncrowned king (Kǒng Zǐ) narrated its teachings.
None did not base their words on the mind of the Dào,
study divine principles to establish teachings,
draw images from the Hé (Yellow River) and Luò (Luò River),
inquire into numbers from the milfoil stalks and tortoise shells,
observe celestial patterns to exhaust change,
and examine human patterns to complete transformation;
only then could they manage territories,
encompass the constant principles,
develop enterprises,
and illuminate the meaning of words.
Therefore, one knows that the Dào is transmitted through the sages by means of literature,
and the sages illuminate the Dào by means of literature,
connecting broadly without limit,
used daily without exhaustion.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"That which stirs all under Heaven is based on words."
The reason why words can stir all under Heaven
is none other than the pattern of the Dào.
Eulogy:
The mind of the Dào is subtle and elusive;
divine principles establish teachings.
The brilliance of the profound sages
illuminates benevolence and filial piety.
The dragon chart presents its form;
the tortoise writing displays its appearance.
Celestial patterns are thus observed;
the people all follow the example.
Chapter Two: Evidence of Sagehood
Those who create are called sages;
those who transmit are called enlightened.
To mold and cast temperament and feelings,
accomplishment lies with the highest sages.
The writings of Fū Zǐ (Kǒng Zǐ)
can be heard,
thus the feelings of the sage
are seen in his words.
The teachings of the former kings
are spread in books and records;
the demeanor of Fū Zǐ (Kǒng Zǐ)
overflows in his maxims.
Therefore, in praising the Táng (Yáo) era from afar,
it was brilliantly prosperous;
in commending the Zhōu dynasty from nearby,
it was richly worth following.
This is evidence that political transformation values literature.
When Zhèng Bó (Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng) entered Chén,
he regarded skillful wording as success;
when Sòng placed the arranged meats,
they valued abundant wording to perform the rites.
This is evidence that events valued literature.
When praising Zǐ Chǎn,
it was said, "Words are sufficient to express the will,
and literature is sufficient to express the words";
when discussing gentlemen generally,
it was said, "Emotions should be sincere,
and words should be skillful."
This is evidence that self-cultivation values literature.
Therefore, when the will is sufficient and the words are patterned,
and the emotions are sincere and the words are skillful,
they are the jade tablets containing potential,
and the golden standards upholding pattern.
To use Zhōu to mirror the sun and moon,
is to reach the extremity of the spirit of the machine;
to complete pattern and measure,
is to think in accord with a talisman.
Sometimes one uses concise words to convey meaning,
or extensive writing to encompass emotions,
or clarifies principles to establish structure,
or hides meaning to conceal function.
Therefore, the *Chūn Qiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) uses a single word for praise and blame,
and the *Sāng Fú* (Mourning Garments) uses lightness to encompass heaviness;
this is using concise words to convey meaning.
The *Bīn Shī* (Odes of Bīn) connects chapters to accumulate phrases,
and the *Rú Xíng* (Conduct of the Scholars) uses elaborate explanation with profuse words;
this is using extensive writing to encompass emotions.
Legal documents use decisiveness to symbolize *Guài* (the breakthrough hexagram),
and writing uses clarity to emulate *Lí* (the radiance hexagram);
this is clarifying principles to establish structure.
The *Sì Xiàng* (Four Symbols) use refined meaning to hide deviously,
and the *Wǔ Lì* (Five Examples) use subtle language to be gently obscure;
this is hiding meaning to conceal function.
Thus, one knows that proliferation and brevity have different forms,
obscurity and clarity have different techniques,
suppressing and drawing out follow the times,
and change and communication adapt to the occasion.
Examining it through Zhōu Gōng and Kǒng Zǐ,
then literature has a teacher.
Therefore, when writing essays, one must seek evidence from the sages;
to understand the sages, one must take the classics as the foundation.
The *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) says, “Discriminating things and rectifying speech,
decisions are then complete”;
the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) says, “Speeches should value substance and brevity,
not only valuing novelty.”
Thus, we know that correct speech is the means to establish discrimination,
substance and brevity are the means to complete an expression;
once expression is complete, there will be no fault of valuing novelty,
once discrimination is established, there will be the beauty of conclusive decisions.
Even if the profound meanings are subtly hidden,
it does not harm its correct speech;
even if the subtle expressions are tactfully obscure,
it does not impair its substance and brevity.
Substance and brevity and subtle expression proceed together,
correct speech and profound meanings are used in conjunction;
the sages’ compositions
can be seen thus.
Yán Hé 顏闔 thought that Zhòng Ní 仲尼 (Confucius) decorated with feathers and painted,
merely engaging in flowery language.
Even if he wanted to criticize the sage,
he could not succeed.
Thus, the elegance and beauty of the sage's writing
indeed holds flowers in its mouth and wears substance on its belt.
The way of Heaven is difficult to hear,
yet some still drill and look up to it;
writings are visible,
so how can one not think about them?
If one seeks evidence from the sages to establish one's words,
then writing will be close to perfection.
The eulogy says:
The ultimate of subtlety produces wisdom,
sagacity and intelligence are the only rulers.
Profound principles become the writing,
outstanding energy becomes the brilliance.
The mirror hangs like the sun and moon,
the language is as rich as mountains and seas.
A hundred years of shadow pass quickly,
a thousand years of heart remains.
Chapter Three: Taking the Classics as the Foundation
The three ultimate, constant teachings,
the books of which are called *Jīng* 經 (Classics).
The *Jīng*,
are the eternal and ultimate Way,
the imperishable great teachings.
Thus, they imitate Heaven and Earth,
emulate ghosts and spirits,
coordinate the order of things,
establish the norms for humans,
penetrate the obscure regions of spiritual nature,
and exhaust the marrow of writing.
The *Sān Fén* 三墳 of the imperial age,
the *Wǔ Diǎn* 五典 of the emperor dynasties,
augmented by the *Bā Suǒ* 八索,
extended by the *Jiǔ Qiū* 九丘,
over ages of misty obscurity,
their branches and streams became numerous and confused,
until Fūzǐ 夫子 (Confucius) edited and narrated them,
and then the great treasures all shone.
Thus, the *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) displays the *Shí Yì* 十翼 (Ten Wings),
the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) marks the seven observations,
the *Shī* 詩 (Book of Odes) lists the four beginnings,
the *Lǐ* 禮 (Book of Rites) rectifies the *Wǔ Jīng* 五經 (Five Classics),
and the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) has five examples.
The meaning is thus molded by human nature and emotion,
and the language is crafted by literary principles,
therefore they can open learning and nourish righteousness,
brightly illuminating with harmony.
However, the mind of the Way is subtle,
the plans of the sages are outstanding and unique,
the walls and courtyard are heavily layered,
inhaling and exhaling is naturally deep.
It is like a ten-thousand *jūn* 鈞 (unit of weight) great bell,
without any small ringing sounds.
The *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) only discusses Heaven,
entering the spiritual and achieving practical application.
Thus, the *Xì* 繫 (Commentary) states that its meaning is far-reaching and its language elegant,
its words hit the mark and its affairs are hidden;
the leather straps were broken three times,
indeed it is the abyss of the black dragon for the wise.
The *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) truly records speeches,
but its commentaries and explanations are vast and obscure;
if one understands the *Ěryǎ* 爾雅 (Approaching Correctness),
then the meaning of the text becomes clear.
Thus, Zǐxià 子夏 (a disciple of Confucius) praised the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents),
shining like the alternating brightness of the sun and moon,
distinct like the scattered movements of the stars,
meaning it is brightly illuminating.
The *Shī* 詩 (Book of Odes) mainly expresses intentions,
its commentaries and explanations are the same as the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents),
spreading wind-like influence and expressing sentiments,
ornate language and surprising metaphors,
gentle and mild in recitation,
daring to most closely attach to deep feelings.
The *Lǐ* 禮 (Book of Rites) establishes the forms,
based on events, it carves out the norms,
its chapters and sections are delicate and intricate,
only after grasping it does it become manifest,
gathering and arranging fragmented words,
nothing is not a treasure.
The *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) discriminates principles,
a single character reveals a meaning,
five *shí* 石 (units of weight) and six *yì* 鷁 (boats),
using detail and omission to form the writing;
*zhìmén* 雉門 (city gate) with two watchtowers,
using sequence to make the intent clear;
its tactful chapters conceal the will,
truly it is profound.
With the *Shàngshū* 尚書 (Book of Documents), browsing the text feels misleading,
but seeking the principle is straightforward;
with the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals), observing the language immediately understands,
but inquiring into the meaning is obscure.
These are the special qualities of the sage’s writing,
the different forms of exterior and interior.
As for the roots being deep and firm,
the branches and leaves being tall and lush,
the language being concise but the meaning abundant,
the events being near but the metaphors being far,
therefore what has passed is old,
but the remaining taste is new every day,
later scholars pursue and acquire it, yet are not late,
earlier scholars have long used it, yet are not first,
it can be said to be Mt. Tài 泰 (mountain) raining everywhere,
and the river irrigating a thousand *lǐ* 里 (unit of distance).
Therefore, for discussions, explanations, prefaces,
the *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) commands the lead;
for imperial edicts, pronouncements, memorials,
the *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) initiates the source;
for *fù* 賦 (rhapsodies), *sòng* 頌 (eulogies), *gē* 謌 (songs), and *zàn* 讚 (praises),
the *Shī* 詩 (Book of Odes) establishes the foundation;
for *míng* 銘 (inscriptions), *lěi* 誄 (dirges), *zhēn* 箴 (admonitions), and *zhù* 祝 (invocations),
the *Lǐ* 禮 (Book of Rites) governs the beginning;
for historical accounts, biographies, alliances, and proclamations,
the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) is the root;
together, they exhaust height to set up the markers,
exhaust distance to open up the boundaries,
therefore the hundred schools leap forward,
ultimately entering within the circle.
If one receives the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) to make the models,
draws from the *Yǎ* 雅 (elegant) to enrich the words,
it is like using a mountain to cast bronze,
and boiling the sea to make salt.
Therefore, if the writing can take the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) as the foundation,
the style will have six meanings:
first, the emotion is deep and not perverse,
second, the air is pure and not mixed,
third, the events are trustworthy and not exaggerated,
fourth, the meaning is steadfast and does not turn back,
fifth, the style is concise and not uncultivated,
sixth, the writing is beautiful and not lewd.
Yángzǐ 楊子 (Yang Xiong) compared carving jade to make a vessel,
to the *Wǔ Jīng* 五經 (Five Classics) containing writing.
Writing is established through conduct,
conduct is transmitted through writing,
the four teachings come first,
form and substance complement each other,
advancing virtue and establishing reputation,
nothing does not take the sages as a teacher;
but establishing words and cultivating language,
few can take the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) as the foundation.
Therefore, the Chu 楚 (state) is flamboyant and the Han 漢 (dynasty) is extravagant,
the bad habits flow and do not return,
rectifying the end and returning to the root,
would that not be excellent!
The eulogy says:
The three ultimate, constant Way,
the teachings are deep and examine antiquity.
Achieving transformation and returning to one,
dividing the teachings into five.
Molding the spiritual nature,
the profound storehouse of writing.
How deep, how melting,
the ancestor of all words.
Chapter Four: Orthodox and Apocryphal
The divine way explains the obscure,
the mandate of Heaven is subtly revealed,
the dragon-horse appeared and the *Dà Yì* 大易 (Great Book of Changes) arose,
the divine turtle appeared and the *Hóng Fàn* 洪範 (Great Plan) shone.
Thus, the *Xìcí* 繫辭 (Appended Remarks) says, “The river emitted a chart,
the Luo 洛 (river) emitted a text,
the sages patterned themselves after them,”
this is what it means.
But the world is far and the writing is hidden,
people like to create falsehoods and exaggerations,
though the true still exists,
the false also relies on it.
The *Liù Jīng* 六經 (Six Classics) are clearly displayed,
while the *Wěi Hòu* 緯候 (Apocryphal Texts) are densely layered;
the *Xiào* 孝 (Classic of Filial Piety) and *Lún* 論 (Analects) are brilliantly clear,
while the *Gōu Chèn* 鉤讖 (Occult Prophecies) are luxuriant;
examining the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) and verifying with the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha),
their falsity is fourfold:
that the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) complete the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
is like weaving,
where silk and hemp are not mixed,
and cloth is then made;
now the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) are correct and the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) are strange,
differing by thousands of *lǐ* 里,
that is the first falsity.
The *Jīng* 經 (Classics) are manifest,
they are the teachings of the sages;
the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) are hidden,
they are divine instruction;
the teachings of the sages should be broad,
divine instruction should be concise;
but now the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) are more numerous than the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
and divine principles are even more complex,
that is the second falsity.
If commands come from Heaven,
they are then called *fú chèn* 符讖 (tallies and prophecies),
but the eighty-one sections,
are all attributed to Kǒngzǐ 孔子;
this is like Yáo 堯 creating the Green Chart,
and Chāng 昌 making the Red Book,
that is the third falsity.
Before the Shāng 商 and Zhōu 周 dynasties,
charts and records were frequently seen,
at the end of the Chūnqiū 春秋 (Spring and Autumn period),
the various *Jīng* 經 (Classics) were finally complete;
*Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) first, then *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
the structure deviates from weaving,
that is the fourth falsity.
Since the falsities are greatly different,
then the differing meanings are self-evident,
the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) are sufficient for instruction,
what do the *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) add?
Tracing the origin of the appearance of charts and records,
they are the glorious mandate of vast Heaven,
events that correspond with sages,
their meaning is not to be paired with the *Jīng* 經 (Classics).
Therefore, when the Hé 河 (Yellow River) did not produce a chart,
Fūzǐ 夫子 (Confucius) sighed,
if they could be created,
there would be no need for lamentation.
In the past, Kāng Wáng 康王 (King Kang) displayed the Hé Tú 河圖 (Yellow River Chart),
in the Eastern Hall,
so we know that the tallies of previous generations,
were treasured and passed down through the ages,
that Zhòngní 仲尼 (Confucius) compiled,
were merely prefaces and records.
Then, those skilled in techniques,
attached them with deceptive arts,
some explaining Yīnyáng 陰陽 (yin and yang),
some describing disasters and anomalies,
like birds chirping resembling speech,
and insects and leaves forming characters,
the clauses and sections grew luxuriantly,
and they all borrowed the name of the Kǒng 孔 (Confucius) family,
a learned scholar investigated,
and said the forgeries began in the Ài 哀 (Ai) and Píng 平 (Ping) reigns,
the secret treasures of the Eastern Hall,
were confused by official robes of purple and vermillion.
As for the time of Guāngwǔ 光武 (Emperor Guangwu),
he sincerely believed in these arts.
The customs were influenced,
and scholars gathered shoulder to shoulder,
Pèi Xiàn 沛獻 (Pei Xian) collected *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) to understand the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
and Cáo Bāo 曹褒 (Cao Bao) compiled *chèn* 讖 (prophecies) to establish rites,
deviating from the Way and mistaking the Classics,
was already excessive.
Therefore, Huán Tán 桓譚 (Huan Tan) criticized their falsehood,
Yǐn Mǐn 尹敏 (Yin Min) mocked their deep flaws,
Zhāng Héng 張衡 (Zhang Heng) exposed their biased errors,
and Xún Yuè 荀悅 (Xun Yue) clarified their deceitful absurdities,
these four worthies were broadly skilled,
and their discussions were precise.
As for the origins of Xī Nóng 羲農 (Xi Nong), Xuān Hào 軒皞 (Xuan Hao),
the essentials of mountains and rivers, and the pitch pipes,
the tallies of white fish and red crows,
and the omens of yellow silver and purple jade,
the events are abundant and wonderful,
and the language is rich and fertile,
they do not benefit the Classics, but they do assist literature.
Therefore, later writers,
gathered up the excellent blossoms,
Píngzǐ 平子 (Zhang Heng) feared they would mislead learning,
and submitted a memorial to prohibit and cut them off;
Zhòngyù 仲豫 (Xun Yue) regretted their mixture with truth,
and did not allow them to be burned;
the previous generations paired them with the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
therefore they are discussed in detail.
Eulogy:
The Róng 榮 (Rong) River and the Wēn 溫 (Wen) River,
are where charts and *Wěi* 緯 (Apocrypha) were conceived.
The divine treasures are hidden in use,
the principles are obscure and the language is valued.
Through the two Hàn 漢 dynasties,
vermillion and purple rose and fell.
Weed out the cunning and strange,
and select their elegant carvings.
Discussing *Sāo* 騷 (Lament) Fifth
Discussing *Sāo* 騷 (Lament) Fifth
Since the sounds of *Fēng* 風 (Airs) and *Yǎ* 雅 (Odes) have ceased,
no one has been able to extract their threads,
and extraordinary literature has flourished,
with the *Lí Sāo* 離騷 (The Lament)!
It has already soared beyond the poets of the past,
and energetically flown before the writers of *cí* 辭 (rhapsody),
could it be that we are not far from the sages,
and that the people of Chǔ 楚 are exceptionally talented?
In the past, Hàn Wǔ 漢武 (Emperor Wu of Han) loved the *Sāo* 騷 (Lament),
and Huáinán 淮南 (Prince of Huainan) wrote a commentary,
saying, "*Guófēng* 國風 (Airs of the States) is fond of beauty but not licentious,
*Xiǎoyǎ* 小雅 (Little Odes) expresses resentment and criticism without disorder,
as for *Lí Sāo* 離騷 (The Lament),
it can be said to combine both.
It sheds its skin from within filth and turbidity,
and floats beyond dust and grime,
it is purely white though stained without becoming black,
it can contend with the sun and moon for glory."
Bān Gù 班固 (Ban Gu) said, "It exposes talent and flaunts self,
with resentment it drowns in the river;
Yì 羿 (Yi) and Jiāo 澆 (Jiao), and the two Yáo 姚 (Yao) sisters,
do not agree with the *Zuǒ Shì* 左氏 (Zuo Tradition);
Kūnlún 崑崙 (Kunlun) and Xuánpǔ 懸圃 (Hanging Garden),
are not recorded in the meaning of the *Jīng* 經 (Classics);
but its language is beautiful and elegant,
it is the ancestor of *cí fù* 詞賦 (lyrical prose),
though not wise,
it can be called wondrous talent."
Wáng Yì 王逸 (Wang Yi) said, "The poets remonstrate by pulling ears,
Qū Yuán 屈原 (Qu Yuan) is gentle and compliant,
the writing of the *Lí Sāo* 離騷 (The Lament),
relies on the *Jīng* 經 (Classics) to establish its meaning,
riding four dragons with a screen of feathers,
is like riding six dragons at the proper time;
Kūnlún 崑崙 (Kunlun) and the quicksand,
are where *Yǔ Gòng* 禹貢 (Tribute of Yu) surveyed the land;
the *cí fù* 詞賦 (lyrical prose) of famous scholars,
all imitate its appearance,
it can be called gold and jade,
unparalleled for a hundred generations."
And Hàn Xuān 漢宣 (Emperor Xuan of Han) praised it,
saying it all accords with the arts of the *Jīng* 經 (Classics);
Yáng Xióng 揚雄 (Yang Xiong) savored and tasted it,
and also said its form is the same as the *Shī* 詩 (Odes) and *Yǎ* 雅 (Odes).
These four families cite it as comparable to the *Jīng* 經 (Classics),
but Mèngjiān 孟堅 (Ban Gu) said it does not accord with the *Zhuàn* 傳 (Traditions),
praising and criticizing at will,

Conclusion:
Writing reality and pursuing emptiness,
the stele and the *lěi* (誄) are established.
Recording virtue and compiling conduct,
literary embellishments are appropriately gathered.
Observing customs is like seeing a face,
and hearing words is like weeping.
Stone and ink engrave brilliance;
how can the declining shadow be suppressed?
Chapter Thirteen: Dirges and Laments
As for bestowing the posthumous title of Xiàn (憲),
"to die young is called Āi (哀)."
Āi (哀),
means "to rely on."
Grief truly relies on the heart,
therefore it is called Āi (哀).
Using words to express grief,
is generally a lament for those of lower status,
thus it is not used for the elderly,
but certainly applied to those who die young.
In the past, when the three good men died for Qín (秦),
even a hundred men could not redeem them.
The circumstances were equally premature and tragic,
and the "Huáng Niǎo" (黃鳥) expressed grief.
Indeed, it was a poet’s expression of grief!
When Hàn Wǔ (漢武) performed the fēngshàn (封禪) ceremony,
and Huò Shàn (霍嬗) died suddenly,
the emperor was saddened and composed a poem,
which was also a type of eulogy.
Coming down to the Later Hàn (後漢),
when the Rǔyáng (汝陽) Prince died,
Cuī Yuán’s (崔瑗) eulogy
began to change the previous style.
However, "stepping into the gate of ghosts"
is strange and not eloquent;
"riding dragons and clouds"
is immortal and not sorrowful.
Moreover, the concluding chapter in five-character lines
somewhat resembles a ballad,
and also vaguely resembles Hàn Wǔ (漢武).
As for Sū Shùn (蘇順) and Zhāng Shēng (張升),
both wrote eulogies,
and although they expressed their literary talents,
they did not fully express their heartfelt sincerity.
Among the Jian'an (建安) eulogies,
only Wèi Cháng (偉長) was relatively good.
The "Xíng Nǚ" (行女) piece
sometimes has a sense of sorrow.
When Pān Yuè (潘岳) continued to write,
he truly embodied its beauty.
Observing his thoughtful considerations and varied diction,
his poignant emotions and sorrowful bitterness,
his narration of events like biographies,
and his concluding words imitating poetry,
with concise four-character verses,
there are few relaxed sentences.
Thus, he could achieve righteousness and gentleness in his writing,
adhering to the old form while embracing new ideas.
"Jīn Lù" (金鹿) and "Zé Lán" (澤蘭)
have no successors.
The main theme of eulogies in general
is that emotion centers on pain and grief,
and the words exhaust the feelings of cherishing.
Because the young have not achieved virtue,
praise is limited to discerning intelligence;
because the weak are not capable of handling affairs,
lamentations are added to their physical appearance.
Concealing one’s feelings and composing the text makes the matter appropriate,
while observing the text and attaching one’s heart to it makes the style extravagant.
An extravagant style of writing
may be beautiful, but it is not sorrowful;
it must make the emotions meet with grief,
and the words draw tears,
then it is valuable.
Diào (弔) means "to arrive."
The *Shī* (詩) says,
"The spirits have come to offer condolences."
It means the spirits have arrived.
When a noble person determines the posthumous title at the end of life,
the matter is most extreme, the reason most sorrowful,
therefore, the guest's consolation to the host
is expressed by saying "to arrive."
To be overwhelmed by water or to violate the proper way
are reasons not to offer condolences.
Also, the water disaster in Sòng (宋) and the fire in Zhèng (鄭),
where messengers conveyed condolences,
were national disasters that caused the death of the people,
so everyone offered condolences.
When Jìn (晉) built the Tái (臺) Tower,
and Qí (齊) attacked Yān (燕) city,
Shǐ Zhào (史趙) and Sū Qín (蘇秦)
turned congratulations into condolences,
oppressing the people and creating enemies
are also ways to ruin.
All such examples
are situations where condolences are appropriate.
Sometimes, people die from arrogance and nobility,
or from narrow-minded anger and violating the proper way,
or having aspirations but lacking opportunity,
or possessing talent but burdened with difficulties;
to remember and console them
are all called diào (弔).
Since Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) floated on the Xiāng (湘) River,
expressing his frustration in "Diào Qū" (弔屈),
the structure was thorough and the content factual,
the words were clear and the reasoning sorrowful;
it was the pioneering work.
As for Sīmǎ Xiāngrú's (司馬相如) "Diào Èr Shì" (弔二世),
it was entirely in the rhapsody style.
Huán Tán (桓譚) believed that its words were mournful
and made readers sigh.
The concluding chapter was essential and poignant,
decisive and capable of evoking sorrow.
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) "Diào Qū" (弔屈),
showed accumulated thought but lacked merit,
its intent was deeply rooted in "Fǎn Sāo" (反騷),
so the rhyme and rhythm were dull and ponderous.
Bān Biāo (班彪) and Cài Yōng (蔡邕)
were both quick at delivering their messages,
but merely shadowed the Jiǎ (賈) style,
making it difficult to run alongside him.
Hú (胡) and Ruǎn’s (阮) "Diào Yí Qí" (弔夷齊)
praised without reservation;
Wáng Càn’s (王粲) work
criticized and rebuked skillfully.
Thus, Hú (胡) and Ruǎn (阮) admired their purity,
while Wáng Zǐ (王子) lamented their narrow-mindedness,
each according to their own inclinations.
Mí Héng's (禰衡) "Diào Píng Zǐ" (弔平子)
was elaborate and graceful, yet light and airy;
Lù Jī's (陸機) "Diào Wèi Wǔ" (弔魏武)
was skillfully arranged and elaborately written.
After these,
there has been nothing worth mentioning.
Although diào (弔) has ancient roots,
refined language had not yet been created.
If refinement goes too far and the rhythm becomes loose,
it transforms into a rhapsody.
It is essential to correct the meaning to align with reason,
reveal virtue and block transgression,
clearly distinguish praise and blame,
and to be sorrowful and righteous,
then there will be no violation of ethics.
Commentary says:
The sorrow of the words
lies in those who are young and tender.
To sprout but not blossom
has been a cause of grief since ancient times.
Even with great talent,
losing direction and control
is a cause for grief for thousands of years,
and is conveyed through allegorical language.
Miscellaneous Writings, Fourteenth
The sons of wisdom and skill,
the men of broad learning and elegance,
their refined language overflows from their words,
and their words are filled with spirit.
To cultivate a garden of literary emotions
results in new and unique qualities every day.
Sòng Yù (宋玉), possessing talent,
somewhat defied convention.
He first created "Duì Wèn" (對問)
to express his aspirations,
freeing his mind in the vastness,
which was driven by his spirit.
When M 枚 Chéng (枚乘) displayed his brilliance,
he first created "Qī Fā" (七發),
rich in language and cloud-like structure,
extravagant and awe-inspiring.
"Qī Fā" (七發) originates from the seven orifices,
arising from desires and passions,
starting with indulgence and ending with correction,
so it is a warning to the sons of the wealthy.
Yáng Xióng (揚雄), with deep thought and broad writing,
had deep learning and comprehensive descriptions.
He composed fragmented sentences and jade-like words,
and first created "Lián Zhū" (連珠),
where words are linked like pearls.
Although small, they are bright and lustrous.
These three,
are branches of literature,
and creations of leisure and recreation.
Following "Dui Wen" (《對問》, "Questions and Answers"),
Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) imitated and expanded upon it,
calling it "Kè Nàn" (《客難》, "Difficulties for the Guest"),
entrusting ancient examples to console his aspirations,
being detached yet articulate.
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) "Jiě Cháo" (《解嘲》, "Dispelling Ridicule"),
mixed with jesting,
circling back to explain himself,
was also quite skillfully done.
Bān Gù's (班固) "Bīn Xì" (《賓戲》, "Guest's Jest"),
contained the splendor of elegant expression;
Cuī Yīn's (崔駰) "Dá Zhǐ" (《達旨》, "Expressing Intent"),
displayed the refinement of classical language;
Zhāng Héng's (張衡) "Yìng Jiàn" (《應間》, "Responding to Interrogation"),
was subtle yet elegant;
Cuī Shí's (崔寔) "Kè Jī" (《客譏》, "Guest's Criticism"),
was organized yet subtly simple;
Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) "Shì Huì" (《釋誨》, "Explaining Admonition"),
possessed profound substance and radiant prose;
and Jǐng Chún's (景純) "Kè Ào" (《客傲》, "Guest's Arrogance"),
revealed emotion and vibrant language.
Although they mutually imitated each other,
they were still among the best of their type.
As for Chén Sī's (陳思) "Kè Wèn" (《客問》, "Guest's Questions"),
the language was elevated, but the reasoning was sparse;
Yǔ Gǎi's (庾敳) "Kè Zī" (《客咨》, "Guest's Inquiries"),
had ambitious ideas but withered prose.
There are so many of this kind
that there is nothing to take from them.
Now, the establishment of this literary form
was to express one's aspirations with passion.
When one's person is thwarted, one relies on the triumph of virtue;
when times are difficult, one finds solace in emotional contentment.
All of these works have hearts as deep as the abyss and mountains,
and literary styles like the lín (麟) and fèng (鳳) (mythical creatures),
which are the grand essentials of establishing the form.
From "Qī Fā" (《七發》, "Seven Stimuli") onward,
authors followed in succession.
Observing Méi Shèng's (枚乘) initial creation,
it was truly outstanding and magnificent.
As for Fù Yì's (傅毅) "Qī Jī" (《七激》, "Seven Excitations"),
it possessed the skill of clear conciseness;
Cuī Yīn's (崔駰) "Qī Yī" (《七依》, "Seven Dependencies"),
attained the cleverness of extensive erudition;
Zhāng Héng's (張衡) "Qī Biàn" (《七辨》, "Seven Discriminations"),
wove together elaborate language;
Cuī Yuán's (崔瑗) "Qī Lì" (《七厲》, "Seven Admonitions"),
established upright principles;
Chén Sī's (陳思) "Qī Qǐ" (《七啟》, "Seven Awakenings"),
took beauty from grandeur;
and Zhòng Xuān's (仲宣, i.e., Wáng Càn 王粲) "Qī Shì" (《七釋》, "Seven Explanations"),
achieved clarity in matters of principle.
From Huán Lín's (桓麟) "Qī Shuō" (《七說》, "Seven Discourses") and
Zuǒ Sī's (左思) "Qī Fěng" (《七諷》, "Seven Satires") onward,
they branched out and followed like shadows,
numbering more than ten families.
Some had beautiful language but divergent meanings,
while others had pure principles but clumsy language.
Observing their general trend,
all of them lavishly discussed palaces and mansions,
and grandly spoke of hunting.
They exhausted extravagant and exotic foods,
and reached the extreme of seductive sounds and sights.
The sweetness moved the bones and marrow,
and the alluring words penetrated the soul and consciousness.
Although they began with indulgence and extravagance,
they ended with dwelling in righteousness.
However, satirizing one thing to advise on a hundred is
a momentum that cannot be reversed.
This is what Zǐ Yún (子雲, i.e., Yáng Xióng 揚雄) meant by "first displaying the sounds of Zhèng (鄭) and Wèi (衛),
and then playing refined music at the end."
Only "Qī Lì" (《七厲》, "Seven Admonitions") narrates worthies
and returns to Confucian doctrines,
and although its language is not outstanding,
its meaning is truly exceptional.
From "Lián Zhū" (《連珠》, "Linked Pearls") onward,
imitators occasionally appeared.
People like Dù Dǔ (杜篤) and Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵),
and the likes of Liú Zhēn (劉珍) and Pān Xù (潘勖),
wanted to pierce bright pearls,
but mostly strung together fish eyes.
It could be said that they were like Shòu Líng (壽陵) crawling,
no longer walking in the manner of Hándān (邯鄲);
a village woman clutching her heart,
not related to Xī Shī's (西施) frown.
Only Shì Héng (士衡, i.e., Lù Jī 陸機) employed his thoughts,
with fresh ideas and nimble writing;
and his composition and sentence structure
were broader than previous works.
Could he have been admiring Zhū Zhòng's (朱仲) four-inch earring?
Now, short compositions are easy to complete,
and leisurely thought can be abundant.
It is enough to make the meaning clear and the language pure,
the subject matter complete and the sound polished,
turning smoothly and continuously,
and then it can be called a pearl.
Examining the miscellaneous writings since the Hàn dynasty,
the names and categories are numerous.
Some are ordinances, announcements, oaths, and inquiries,
others are outlines and summaries of chapters,
others are musical pieces and ballads,
and still others are recitations of satire and songs.
To summarize their names,
they all fall under the category of miscellaneous writings;
to distinguish their meanings,
each enters the realm of discussion.
Grouping them by category creates a connected structure,
so I will not describe them in detail.
Appended Praise:
Great were the former worthies,
with firm learning and abundant talent.
With remaining literary strength,
they flew and fluttered, displaying their skill.
Their techniques and language intertwined and reflected,
glittering like the stars of Orion and the Pleiades.
The heart of admiring a frown
is thereby disturbed.
Chapter Fifteen: Jests and Riddles
Chapter Fifteen: Jests and Riddles
A poem by Ruì Liángfū (芮良夫) says:
"Having their own hearts and minds,
they caused the people to go completely mad."
Indeed, a heart as treacherous as a mountain,
and a mouth as blocked as a river,
resentful emotions are not uniform,
and humorous words are boundless.
In the past, when Huá Yuán (華元) abandoned his armor,
the city dwellers sang songs with glaring eyes;
when Zāng Hē (臧紇) lost a battle,
the people of the state created songs about dwarfs.
Both mocked physical appearances,
turning inner resentment into jesting.
Furthermore, vulgar sayings about silkworms and crabs,
and lewd songs about civet cats,
if they can be used for admonishment,
are recorded in the classics.
Therefore, it is known that humorous sayings and riddling words
are also not to be discarded.
The word "xié (諧)" means "all."
Language that is shallow and meets the customs
brings joy and laughter to all.
In the past, Qí Wēi (齊威) indulged in pleasure,
and Chúnyú Yuè (淳于說) spoke of sweet wine;
Chǔ Xiāng (楚襄) gathered for feasts,
and Sòng Yù (宋玉) composed about a love for beauty.
The intention was subtle satire,
and there was something worth seeing in it.
And Yōu Zhān's (優旃) satire on the painted city,
and Yōu Mèng's (優孟) admonishment about burying the horse,
both used cunning words and embellished explanations
to restrain foolish tyranny.
Therefore, Zǐcháng (子長, i.e., Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷) compiled history
and included a biography of "Huá Jī" (《滑稽》, "Jesters"),
because although their words were distorted,
their intentions returned to righteousness and correctness.
However, since the essence is not elegant,
its current easily becomes corrupt.
Therefore, Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) and Méi Gāo (枚皋),
ate dregs and drank thin wine,
without correcting anything,
but instead slandered and made disrespectful jests.
Therefore, what they called fù (賦)
was actually also pai (俳, jesting).
Being seen as merely entertainers,
they also had regrets.
As for Wèi Wén (魏文) composing "Xiào Shū" (《笑書》, "Book of Laughter") based on jesting tales,
and Xuē Zōng (薛綜) issuing mocking jokes during banquets,
although there was clapping, laughter, and joyful clothing,
it did nothing to benefit the times.
However, even those with beautiful writing
could not avoid being led astray;
things like Pān Yuè's (潘岳) "Chǒu Fù" (《醜婦》, "Ugly Woman"),
and types like Shù Xī's (束晳) "Mài Bǐng" (《賣餅》, "Selling Cakes"),
went even further and imitated them,
numbering in the hundreds.
The jesters of the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties
greatly encouraged each other.
Consequently, Yìng Yáng's (應瑒) nose
was compared to a robber slicing eggs;
and Zhāng Huá's (張華) form
was compared to holding a pestle for hulling grain.
This was truly like noxious weeds,
impairing virtuous words.
Could it not be the reckless laughter of those drowning,
and the wild songs of the convicts?
Yǐn (讔) means yǐn (隱),
or hidden;
using evasive language to conceal meaning,
employing cunning metaphors to indicate matters.
In the past, Huán Shè (還社) sought rescue from the Chǔ (楚) army,
using the metaphor of a dry well and calling it màiqu (麥麴);
Shū Yí (叔儀) begged for grain from the Lǔ (魯) people,
singing about jade pendants and calling out gēng guǐ (庚癸);
Wǔ Jǔ (伍舉) satirized the Jīng (荊) king with a large bird,
a Qí (齊) guest mocked Lord Xuē (薛) with a sea fish,
Zhuāng Jī (莊姬) entrusted her words to the Dragon Tail Star,
Zāng Wén (臧文) mistakenly wrote on a sheepskin coat.
The use of hidden language
is recorded in chronicles and biographies.
The great use of it leads to the rise of governance and benefits the self,
the lesser use of it assists in correcting errors and clarifying doubts.
Indeed, meaning arises from expediency and stratagem,
and matters stem from timely wit and urgency,
together with humorous language,
which can complement each other.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the "Book of Hidden Language" 《隱書》
had eighteen chapters.
Xīn Gù (歆固) compiled the text,
and recorded it at the end of his rhymeprose compositions.
In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ (楚莊) and King Wēi of Qí (齊威)
were by nature fond of hidden language.
As for Dōngfāng Mànqiàn (東方曼倩),
he was particularly skilled in descriptive language.
However, absurd and derogatory language
is of no benefit for guidance or supplementation.
Since the Wèi (魏) dynasty and later,
it has been regarded as something other than acting,
and the cultured's jesting and concealing
has transformed into riddles.
A riddle is
the revolving and alternating of words,
causing confusion and bewilderment.
Sometimes it takes the form of written characters,
or depicted images and items,
subtle tricks to toy with the mind,
shallow observations to flaunt language,
the meaning should be gentle yet upright,
the words should be hidden yet clear.
Xún Qīng's (荀卿) "Ode to the Silkworm" 《蠶賦》
already foreshadowed its form.
During the time of Wèi Wén (魏文) and Chén Sī (陳思),
it was concise and precise;
the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng (高貴鄉公)
extensively cited various items.
Though there was some ingenuity,
its use deviated from the grand and far-reaching.
When we observe the ancient use of hidden language,
its principles encompass essential affairs.
How could it be a childish jest,
slapping thighs and laughing aloud?
However, the presence of humor and hidden meaning in literary compositions
is like the presence of minor tales among the Nine Schools;
they are gathered by the writers of unofficial histories
to broaden sight and sound.
If one imitates them without end,
then one would be like shaving the head and baring the shoulders to enter the room,
the friendship of Zhān Mèng (旃孟) would be like stone!
In praise:
The mocking and concealing of the ancients
revived dangers and relieved weariness.
Though there are silk and hemp,
do not discard coarse grasses.
Understanding the meaning and fitting the time,
it greatly benefits admonishments and warnings.
Empty jesting and buffoonery
greatly ruin virtuous sounds.
Chapter Sixteen: History and Biographies
In the opening of the primitive mists,
the ages stretched out long and far.
To reside in the present and know the past,
it is through the records.
In the era of Xuānyuán (軒轅),
there was the historian Cāng Jié (蒼頡),
whose duty was to oversee writing.
Its origins are long ago.
The *Qū Lǐ* (曲禮) says:
"Historians carry brushes."
The historian,
is a messenger;
holding a brush to the left and right,
they are used to record.
In ancient times, the left historian recorded words,
the right historian wrote matters.
Words that pass through the classics are the *Shàngshū* (尚書),
matters that pass through the classics are the *Chūnqiū* (春秋).
The Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) flowed into the *Diǎn Mó* (典謨),
the Xià (夏) and Shāng (商) were recorded in proclamations and oaths.
When the Zhōu (周) mandate was renewed,
Duke Jī (姬) established the laws,
drawing from the Three Dynasties to distribute the calendar,
and stringing together the four seasons to connect events.
The feudal lords established states,
each with its own state history,
manifesting good and abhorring evil,
establishing a reputation for them.
Since King Píng (平) was weak,
his administration did not reach correctness,
rules and regulations were scattered and disordered,
and moral principles were abandoned.
In the past, Master Kǒng (孔) lamented the deficiency of the kingly way,
and grieved the decline of this culture,
dwelling in silence to sigh at the phoenix,
and weeping at the unicorn in the streets.
Therefore, he went to the grand master to correct the *Yǎ* (雅) and *Sòng* (頌),
and relied on the history of Lǔ (魯) to revise the *Chūnqiū* (春秋),
raising gains and losses to show promotion and demotion,
and examining survival and extinction to mark encouragement and warning;
praise seen in a single word
is worth more than carriages and official hats;
blame found in a single phrase
is like a punishment deeper than axes and hatchets.
However, the wise intent is deep and hidden,
the classic text is gentle and restrained,
Qiū Míng (丘明), who was contemporary to Master Kǒng,
truly grasped the subtle words;
therefore, he traced the origin and reached the end,
creating the commentary style.
Commentary,
is to transmit;
transmitting and receiving the classic intent,
to bestow it upon posterity,
truly the wings and feathers of the sagely texts,
and the crown and hat of the records.
Even in the era of alliances and counter-alliances,
the office of the historian still existed.
When Qín conquered the seven kingdoms,
the Warring States period had its *Cè*.
These likely recorded events without narrating them,
hence their simple and concise titles.
When Hàn destroyed Yíng and Xiàng,
after years of military achievements,
Lù Jiǎ researched the ancient past
and wrote *Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū*.
Then came Tài Shǐ Tán,
who only kept records,
and his son, Zǐcháng, continued his aspirations,
carefully arranging the achievements of emperors.
To compare him to Yáo using *Diǎn*,
would place him among the worthy officials;
to follow Kǒngzǐ in titling classics,
would make his writing unprofound.
Thus, he took the model of *Lǚ Lǎn*,
generally calling them *Jì*,
the name *Jìgāng*,
which is also a grand title.
Therefore, *běnjì* is used to narrate emperors and kings,
*lièzhuàn* to compile accounts of lords and nobles,
*Bā Shū* to elaborate on political systems,
*Shí Biǎo* to chronicle years and ranks.
Although different from ancient forms,
they achieve an orderly account of events.
Indeed, his work embodies the principle of recording without concealment,
the talent of broad learning and eloquent reasoning,
the tendency to love the unusual and rebel against convention,
and the flaw of scattered and imprecise organization,
as Shū Pí has discussed in detail.
When Bān Gù wrote the *Hàn Shū*,
he followed the previous work.
Observing Sīmǎ Qiān's writing,
his thoughts were more than half based on reality.
His *Shí Zhì* are comprehensive and rich,
his prefaces and eulogies magnificent and beautiful,
his elegance refined,
truly leaving behind a lasting flavor.
As for his adherence to the classics as a standard and the sagely as a model,
his merit in establishing a complete framework,
his fault in neglecting relatives to praise others,
and his offense of seeking bribes and selling his pen,
public reason has judged thoroughly.
Consider how Zuǒ Qiūmíng connected events,
interspersing them within the *Jīng*,
making the writing concise,
but leaving the clans difficult to understand.
When Sīmǎ Qiān wrote individual biographies,
people began to see detailed and easy-to-read accounts,
and subsequent narrators followed his example.
When Xiàohuì delegated authority
and Empress Lǚ took control of the government,
the historians Bān followed suit in their *Jì*,
both violating the truth of the classics.
Why?
Since Páo Xī,
there has never been a female emperor.
The Hàn dynasty's fortune was such that
it is difficult to make it a model for later generations.
"The hen does not announce the morning,"
was the first oath of King Wǔ;
"Women should not participate in state affairs,"
was the covenant set forth by Duke Huán of Qí;
Empress Xuān brought chaos to Qín,
and the Lǚ clan endangered Hàn.
It is not only that political affairs should not be entrusted lightly,
but also that titles should be carefully considered.
Zhāng Héng, as the historian,
either agreed with Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
or wanted to establish *Jì* for the two empresses who leveled the imperial line in the first year,
which is also greatly mistaken.
This is also a great error.
Although Zǐ Hóng's lineage is spurious,
he was still the successor to Emperor Xiàohuì;
Rúzǐ was indeed insignificant,
but he did succeed Emperor Píng.
These two sons can be recorded,
so why the two empresses?
As for the *Hòu Hàn Shū*'s *Jì* and *Zhuàn*,
they originated from the *Dōng Guān*.
The works of Yuán and Zhāng
were biased and uneven.
The writings of Xuē and Xiè
were superficial, flawed, and lacked credibility.
If one seeks detail and accuracy, like Sīmǎ Biāo's work,
or precision and appropriateness, like Huá Qiáo's,
then those are the best.
During the Wei Dynasty,
records and biographies emerged in abundance.
Works such as the *Yáng Qiū* and *Wèi Lüè*,
and the *Jiāng Biǎo* and *Wú Lù*,
were either vehemently controversial and difficult to verify,
or superficial and lacking in essential points.
Only Chén Shòu's *Sān Zhì*
had a refined and balanced style,
leading Xún and Zhāng to compare him to Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
which is not an undeserved compliment.
As for the books of the Jìn dynasty,
they were entrusted to the *Zhù Zuò*.
Lù Jī began the work but did not complete it,
Wáng Sháo continued it but did not finish.
Gān Bǎo, in narrating *Jì*,
sought to be thorough in correctness and order;
Sūn Shèng's *Yáng Qiū*
aimed for skillful summarization.
Based on the *Chūnqiū* and its *Jīngzhuàn*,
he cited examples to explain general principles.
From *Shǐ Jì* and *Hàn Shū* onward,
there has been no standard.
It was not until Dèng Càn's *Jìn Jì*
that regulations were first established.
Furthermore, it abandoned the Hàn and Wèi models,
and took the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties as its norms.
Even though it was a provincial work from Xiāngzhōu,
it still aspired to the model of *Diǎn Mó*.
When Ān Guó established precedents,
they followed Dèng's regulations.
Originally, the creation of written records
must encompass the hundred schools
and be passed down for thousands of years,
manifesting prosperity and decline,
providing a mirror for rise and fall,
so that the institutions of a generation
may endure with the sun and moon,
and the deeds of kings and hegemons
may last as long as heaven and earth.
Therefore, at the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
the office of the historian was highly regarded.
The records and statistics from the commanderies and kingdoms
were first gathered in the office of the Grand Historian,
so that he could have a detailed understanding of the state.
Examining the stone chambers,
opening the golden cabinets,
unrolling the silk,
inspecting the bamboo slips,
was to ensure broad and practiced research into the past.
Therefore, in establishing principles and selecting words,
one should rely on the classics to set the standard;
in encouraging or discouraging, rewarding or punishing,
one must adhere to the sages as the foundation;
only then can interpretation and evaluation be clear and orderly,
and excessive or unfair judgments be avoided.
However, with annals and biographies as the format,
compiling events chronologically,
the writing should not be a general discussion,
but rather based on facts.
As years pass, it becomes difficult to closely examine similarities and differences,
and as events accumulate, it becomes easy to overlook beginnings and endings;
this is indeed the difficulty of comprehensive compilation.
Sometimes, the same event is attributed to several individuals,
and several people share the credit.
To record it in both accounts would lead to redundancy,
while to mention only one would be incomplete;
this is the difficulty of proper allocation.
Therefore, Zhāng Héng pointed out the errors and exaggerations of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
and Fù Xuán criticized the excessive detail of the *Hòu Hàn Shū*;
these are all examples of this kind.
As for recounting the distant past,
the further back in time, the more falsehoods there are.
Gōngyáng Gāo said,
"Transmitted accounts differ."
Xún Kuàng stated,
"Record what is recent and omit what is distant."
For doubtful passages, it is better to leave them out and
value reliable history.
However, people generally love the unusual,
not caring about true principles.
In transmitting accounts, they want to magnify the events,
and in recording the distant past, they want to detail the traces,
thus abandoning what is the same and embracing what is different,
making conjectures and citing side accounts.
"What the old history does not have,
my book will transmit"—
this is the source of errors and exaggerations,
and the great blight of recounting the distant past.
As for recording events of the same era,
it is easy for falsehoods to arise,
even with the subtle words of Duke Dìng and Duke Āi,
because of worldly interests and harms.
Families with meritorious achievements,
even the mediocre are fully embellished;
scholars who have suffered setbacks,
even those of great virtue are slandered and buried.
Bestowing frost or warmth,
cold or heat, is at the tip of the pen;
this is the injustice of contemporary records,
which is lamentable.
Therefore, recounting the distant past leads to such falsehoods,
and recording the recent past leads to such distortions;
to analyze principles and remain impartial,
one must have a pure heart!
To respect the worthy and conceal [their] faults
was indeed the sagacious intention of Ní Fù 尼父;
for minor flaws cannot tarnish a jade ornament.
To punish and warn against the wicked
is truly the straightforward writing of a good historian.
When a farmer sees weeds,
he will certainly hoe them out.
Such principles
are a standard for all ages.
As for the skill of seeking simplicity in complexity,
the importance of adhering to facts and discarding the bizarre,
the clear order of beginning and end,
the careful consideration of precedents and examples,
if one understands their main points,
then all principles can be connected.
However, the responsibility of history
is to encompass an entire era,
to bear the responsibility for everything within the realm,
and to incur the greatest amount of censure.
To hold the writing brush and bear the burden
is more laborious than anything else.
Si Qian 遷固 (Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷 and Bān Gù 班固) were thorough,
yet were consistently criticized by later generations.
If one indulges emotions and deviates from correctness,
the writing will be perilous!
Commentary:
History began with Xuān Yuán 軒轅,
and its structure was perfected by Zhōu 周 and Kǒng 孔.
The world has been recorded in these books;
good and evil are all included.
Praise is bestowed, and blame is meted out;
for ten thousand ages, spirits are stirred.
The style follows Qiū Míng 丘明,
and the honesty returns to Nán Dǒng 南董.
The Philosophers, Number Seventeen
The philosophers are
books that reveal the will of those who entered the Way.
The highest is to establish virtue;
the next is to establish words.
The masses who live together
suffer from confusion and obscurity;
the gentleman who lives in the world
is concerned that his reputation and virtue are not manifest.
Only outstanding talents
shine brightly and leave behind writings,
spreading their names
and hanging them like the sun and moon.
In the past, Fēng Hòu 風后, Lì Mù 力牧, and Yī Yǐn 伊尹
all belonged to this category.
Their written accounts
are ancient sayings
recorded during the Warring States period.
When Yù Xióng 鬻熊 understood the Way,
and Wén Wáng 文王 consulted him,
the remaining writings and anecdotes
were recorded as *Yùzǐ* 《鬻子》.
Among the philosophers,
nothing predates this.
When Bó Yáng 伯陽 understood ritual,
and Zhòng Ní 仲尼 inquired of him,
he then arranged morality and virtue
to be the foremost of the hundred schools.
Thus, Yù was merely a literary friend,
while Lǐ 李 was actually Kǒng's 孔 teacher.
Sages and worthies coexisted,
but the classics and the philosophers diverged into different streams.
During the time of the Seven Warring States,
talented individuals emerged in swarms.
Mèng Kē 孟軻 embraced Confucianism with humility,
Zhuāng Zhōu 莊周 expounded the Way and soared freely,
Mò Dí 墨翟 adhered to a frugal and steadfast doctrine,
Yǐn Wén 尹文 assessed the correspondence between names and realities,
the rustic old man governed the state through geographical advantages,
Zōu Zǐ 騶子 cultivated governance through astronomy,
Shēn Shāng 申商 used knives and saws to establish order,
Guǐ Gǔ 鬼谷 used rhetoric to plan meritorious deeds,
Shī Jiǎo 尸佼 comprehensively mastered various techniques,
and the court historians crookedly pieced together street gossip.
Those who followed and branched out
were too numerous to count.
They all flew with eloquence and raced with techniques,
indulging in generous salaries and abundant honors.
When the violent Qín 秦 dynasty used raging fire,
its power blazed like Kūnlún 崑崙 mountain,
but the poison of the flames
did not reach the philosophers.
When Hàn 漢 Chéng 漢成 (Hàn Chéngdì 漢成帝) extensively pondered and
Zǐ Zhèng 子政 collated and proofread,
the *Qī Lüè* 《七略》 then flourished,
and the nine streams gathered like scales,
the bamboo slips that were compiled
numbered more than one hundred and eighty schools.
Until the Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉 dynasties,
authors emerged intermittently,
wild words were preserved,
and trivial sayings were recorded.
Classifying and searching for them
could fill boxes and load wagons.
Although voluminous words accumulated,
the main body is easy to summarize:
describing the Way and discussing governance
are branches of the *Five Classics* 《五經》.
Those that are pure enter the square,
while those that are flawed deviate from the compass.
*Lǐjì‧Yuèlìng* 《禮記‧月令》 takes
from the records of *Lǚshì* 《呂氏》;
*Sān Nián Wèn* 《三年問》 on mourning
copies from the book of *Xúnzǐ* 《荀子》;
these are examples of the pure.
As for Tāng's 湯 question to Jí 棘,
saying that the eyelash of a mosquito has the sound of thunder;
Huì Shī's 惠施 response to the King of Liáng 梁,
saying that on a snail's horn there is a battle with corpses lying prone;
*Lièzǐ* 《列子》 has talk of moving mountains and crossing seas;
*Huáinán* 《淮南》 has sayings of overturning the sky and breaking the earth;
these are examples of the flawed.
Therefore, the world despises the philosophers
for their chaotic and empty exaggerations.
Examining the classic of *Guī Cáng* 《歸藏》,
it greatly clarifies the eccentric and strange,
even claiming that Yì 羿 shot down ten suns
and Héng'é 姮娥 fled to the moon.
The *Yīn Yì* 《殷易》 is like this;
how much more so the philosophers!
As for *Shāng* 《商》 and *Hán* 《韓》,
the "Six Lice" and "Five Vermin,"
abandoning filial piety and discarding benevolence,
the disaster of dismemberment for selling medicine
was not a false occurrence.
Gōngsūn's 公孫 "White Horse" and "Lone Calf,"
with clever words but clumsy logic,
Wèi Mú 魏牟 compared them to owls;
it was not a groundless disparagement.
In the past, Dōngpíng 東平 sought the philosophers' *Shǐjì* 《史記》,
but the Hàn 漢 dynasty did not grant it.
This was because *Shǐjì* 《史記》 contained many military strategies,
while the philosophers mixed in deceitful techniques.
However, learned scholars
should grasp the main points,
examine the flowers and eat the fruit,
discard the heretical and adopt the correct,
and thoroughly discern the discrepancies;
this is also a grand spectacle for students of learning.
Investigating what Mèng (孟) and Xún (荀) described,
their principles are excellent and their language refined;
the chapters of Guǎn (管) and Yàn (晏)
concern matters of fact and their words are polished;
the book of Liè Yǔkòu (列御寇),
has grandeur in spirit and extraordinary brilliance in its writing;
the doctrines of Zōu Zǐ (鄒子),
have extravagant ideas and powerful language;
Mò Dí (墨翟) and Suí Cháo (隨巢),
have clear intentions and simple words;
Shī Jiǎo (尸佼) and Wèi Liáo (尉繚),
have comprehensive strategies but their writing is dull;
*Hé Guān* (鶡冠) is continuous and profound,
frequently expressing deep insights;
*Guǐ Gǔ* (鬼谷) is vast and obscure,
repeatedly circling its meaning;
with acute discernment and eloquent expression,
Wén Zǐ (文子) excels in his abilities;
with concise and refined language,
Yǐn Wén (尹文) grasped its essence;
Shèn Dào (慎到) analyzes with ingenious precision,
Hán Fēi (韓非) is known for the richness of his extensive analogies,
*Lǚ Shì* (呂氏) is far-sighted and comprehensive in its structure,
*Huáinán* (淮南) widely gathers and its writing is beautiful;
this then is to obtain the brilliant essence of a hundred schools,
and the general outline of their diction and spirit.
As for Lù Jiǎ's (陸賈) *Xīn Yǔ* (新語),
Jiǎ Yì's (賈誼) *Xīn Shū* (新書),
Yáng Xióng's (揚雄) *Fǎ Yán* (法言),
Liú Xiàng's (劉向) *Shuō Yuàn* (說苑),
Wáng Fú's (王符) *Qián Fū* (潛夫),
Cuī Shí's (崔寔) *Zhèng Lùn* (正論),
Zhòngcháng's (仲長) *Chāng Yán* (昌言),
Dù Yí's (杜夷) *Yōu Qiú* (幽求),
all expound on the classics,
or elucidate political strategies,
although they bear the name of essays,
they belong to the philosophers.
Why is this?
To broadly understand myriad affairs is to be a philosopher (子),
to appropriately discern a single principle is to be an essay (論);
these all extensively mix various theories,
therefore they enter the stream of philosophical works.
Before the Six States (六國),
it was not far from the sages,
therefore they were able to discourse loftily, surpassing their era,
and opening their own windows.
After the Two Han dynasties (兩漢),
the style and momentum gradually weakened,
although they understood the clear path,
they mostly relied on borrowing.
This is the gradual change from near to far.
Alas!
The person is at odds with the times,
but the will shares the way;
setting one's heart above ten thousand ages,
and sending one's thoughts to a thousand years hence,
gold and stone will decay,
will their voices be silenced?
A eulogy:
A great man living in the world,
cherishes his treasure and stands out in excellence.
Discriminatingly carving the myriad things,
his wisdom encompasses the universe.
Establishing virtue, why hide it?
Holding the Dao, it must be imparted.
The different schools have various explanations,
as if there are boundaries and enclosures.
Discourse: Chapter 18
Now, the establishment of official positions and the division of duties
links high and low positions.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) lowers his jade beads to listen,
and the lords jingle their jade ornaments to attend the court.
They extensively report with words,
and clearly assess based on merit.
Therefore, Yáo consulted the Four Mountains (Sì Yuè),
and Shùn appointed the Eight Talents (Bā Yuán).
They firmly declined the request to refuse again,
and accepted the Yū (俞) assignment with reverence.
Both presented their reports at the imperial court,
not relying on written documents.
Therefore, extensively reporting with words is
the meaning of memorial (zhāng) and petition (biǎo);
clearly assessing based on merit
is the standard for bestowing ranks.
When Tài Jiǎ was newly established,
Yī Yǐn wrote admonishments.
Thinking of returning to Bó (亳),
he again wrote in praise.
Written documents were offered and rejected,
and the matter was thus revealed.
The Zhōu Dynasty (Zhōu Daì) oversaw the two dynasties
and the literary principles became even more prosperous.
With repeated bows and prostrations,
they responded by extolling and receiving gracious commands.
They accepted written documents and received inscribed tablets,
daring to undertake great achievements.
Although speech and writing were not yet distinct,
statements of gratitude and refusal can be seen.
Descending to the Seven Kingdoms (Qī Guó),
the ancient forms were not changed.
When reporting matters to the king,
they all called it “submitting a letter (shàng shū).”
When the Qín Dynasty (Qín Chū) first established regulations,
“letter (shū)” was changed to “memorial (zoù).”
When the Hàn Dynasty (Hàn Daì) established rituals,
there were four categories:
first was memorial (zhāng),
second was report (zoù),
third was petition (biǎo),
and fourth was discussion (yì).
Memorials were used to thank for grace,
reports were used to investigate and impeach,
petitions were used to present requests,
and discussions were used to uphold differing opinions.
The memorial (zhāng)
means to make clear.
The *Book of Odes (Shī)* says:
"To make manifest in Heaven."
Referring to making civilization manifest.
In artifacts,
red and white are called zhāng.
The petition (biǎo)
means to mark.
The *Book of Rites (Lǐ)* has the *Record of Marking (Biǎo Jì)*,
meaning that virtue is manifested in ceremony.
In the form of instruments,
measuring shadows is called biǎo.
The categories of memorial (zhāng) and petition (biǎo)
are likely derived from these.
According to the *Seven Summaries (Qī Lüè)* and the *Arts and Literature (Yì Wén)*
, ballads and songs were certainly recorded;
but memorials (zhāng), reports (zoù), petitions (biǎo), and discussions (yì),
which are the pivot of governing the state,
were omitted and not compiled,
because each had its own precedent
and were distributed among the responsible officials.
In the Former Hàn Dynasty (Qián Hàn Daì), there were few
surviving pieces of memorials of gratitude and refusal.
During the Later Hàn Dynasty (Hoù Hàn Daì), recommendations and selections
required testing through memorials and reports.
Zuǒ Xióng’s written reports
became the model for the central government;
Hú Guǎng’s memorials and reports
were the best in the land;
both were outstanding writers of their time.
Observing Bó Shǐ’s memorial upon visiting the mausoleum
is sufficient to see the beauty of its classic prose.
In the past, when Duke Wén of Jìn (Jìn Wén Gōng) received his investiture,
he declined three times before accepting the mandate.
Therefore, at the end of the Hàn Dynasty, declinations of office
were decided based on three refusals.
Cáo Gōng declared that petitions should not exceed three refusals,
nor should they be extravagant and flowery.
Therefore, the memorials of the early Weì Dynasty (Weì Chū)
were based on real events and true substance.
Seeking their embellished elegance
would be insufficient to appreciate them.
As for Wén Jǔ’s recommendation of Mí Héng,
the spirit soars and the expression takes flight;
and Kǒng Míng’s address to the later lord (Hoù Zhǔ),
expressing his aspirations fully and articulating the text smoothly.
Although refinement and substance have different purposes,
both are heroes of petitions.
Lín Yǔ’s memorials and petitions
were praised in their time;
and Kǒng Zhāng was known for his vigor,
which was his hallmark.
Chén Sī’s memorials
uniquely surpassed all others.
Observing their comprehensive structure and regulated rhythm,
clear language and manifest intent,
skillful adaptation to circumstances,
and spontaneous generation of interest with changing situations,
he held the reins with ease,
thus able to respond flexibly to circumstances.
As for the brushwork of the early Jìn Dynasty (Jìn Chū),
Zhāng Huá was unparalleled.
His three refusals of the ducal title
were thorough in reasoning and concise in language,
quoting principles and comparing matters,
always finding the perfect match.
The world treasures the wren,
but no one cares for memorials and petitions.
And Yáng Gōng’s *Refusal of the Opening of the Fǔ (府)*
was praised in previous discussions;
and Yǔ Gōng’s *Declination of the Secretariat (Zhōng Shū)*
was truly admired in times past.
Arranging aspirations and clarifying categories
possesses literary refinement.
Liú Kūn’s *Exhortation to Advance*,
and Zhāng Jùn’s *Self-Preface*,
with their straightforward literary style,
are both beautiful examples of presenting matters.
Considering the use of memorials and petitions,
they are for responding and extolling in the royal court,
and revealing one's innermost feelings.
They refine oneself,
and also glorify the nation.
Memorials presented at the palace gate
should be clear in their model and pattern;
petitions submitted to the imperial presence
should have a radiant structure and style.
Evaluating according to name and assessing based on reality,
with writing as the foundation.
Therefore, the format of memorials should be brilliant and elegant,
with the intent to follow classics and models;
essential but not terse,
clear but not shallow.
The form of petitions is often comprehensive,
with emotions and falsehoods frequently changing.
It is necessary to use refined language to cultivate their style,
and pure writing to express their beauty.
However, in earnestness, words are driven by the heart,
while in extravagance, feelings are constrained by the writing.
It is necessary to ensure that complexity and brevity are balanced,
that refinement and substance are in equilibrium,
and that the expression is not stilted,
then it will be in harmony.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Control it with the heart,
and bind it with words."
This conveys the same idea.
Xún Qīng believed that "observing a person's beautiful language,
adorned with elaborate and embroidered writing,"
can also be compared to this!
Praise:
Extensively reporting at the vermilion palace,
offering proposals at the embroidered screen.
Words must be upright and clear,
and meaning must be grand and magnificent.
Respectful and proper in ceremonial form,
well-organized in beginning and end.
The gentleman embraces writing,
and his rhetoric is elegant.
Reports and Petitions, Twenty-third
To repeatedly consult and deliberate,
this is called "wéi yì" (為議, to deliberate).
"Yì zhī yán yí" (議之言宜, the language of deliberation should be appropriate),
means to carefully consider what is appropriate for the matter.
In the *Yì* (易, Book of Changes), *Jié Guà* (節卦, Hexagram of Restraint) states,
"Jūnzǐ yǐ zhìdù shù,
yì déxíng" (君子以制度數，議德行, the noble person establishes measures and numbers to deliberate on virtue and conduct).
The *Zhōu Shū* (周書, Book of Zhou) says,
"Yì shì yǐ zhì,
zhèng nǎi fú mí" (議事以制，政乃弗迷, deliberate on affairs with regulations, and the government will not be confused).
Deliberation values restraint,
which is the essence of the classics.
In the past, Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) spoke of the Míngtái (明臺, Bright Terrace) deliberation of Xuānyuán (軒轅),
so its origins are ancient.
During the disaster of the great flood,
Yáo (堯) consulted the Sì Yuè (四岳, Four Peaks);
for the appointment of the Zhai Kui (宅揆, Residence Regulator),
Shùn (舜) surveyed the Wǔ Rén (五人, Five Men).
The rise of the Three Dynasties
involved consulting even the woodcutters.
The *Chūnqiū* (春秋, Spring and Autumn Annals) explained Sòng (宋),
and Lǔ Xī (魯僖) participated in the deliberation.
When Zhào Líng (趙靈) adopted the clothing of the Hú (胡) people,
Jì Fù (季父) debated the matter;
when Shāng Yāng (商鞅) reformed the laws,
Gān Lóng (甘龍) argued back and forth.
Although the regulations were countless,
the similarities and differences were enough to observe.
Up until the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the practice of "bó yì" (駁議, refuting deliberation) was first established.
"Bó" (駁, refuting)
means "zà" (雜, mixed).
Refuting deliberation is not pure,
therefore it is called "bó" (駁, refuting).
Since the civilization of the two Hàn dynasties,
models have been illuminated and prepared,
and many capable people
spoke their minds in court.
If Jiǎ Yí's (賈誼) arguments can represent all scholars,
then he can be said to be swift in deliberation.
As for Wūqiū's (吾丘) refutation of carrying bows,
Ānguó's (安國) defense against the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
Jiǎ Juānzhī's (賈捐之) presentation on Zhūyá (朱崖),
and Liú Xīn's (劉歆) defense of his ancestors,
although the substance and style differed,
they grasped the essentials of the matter.
If Zhang Mǐn's (張敏) judgment on slight insults,
Guō Gōng's (郭躬) deliberation on unauthorized executions,
Chéng Xiǎo's (程曉) refutation of school affairs,
Sīmǎ Zhī's (司馬芝) deliberation on currency,
Hé Zēng's (何曾) exemption of women from certain duties,
and Qín Xiù's (秦秀) determination of Jiǎ Chōng's (賈充) posthumous title,
the facts were appropriate and justified,
and can be said to have mastered the form of deliberation.
During the Hàn dynasty, 應劭 (Yìng Shào) was the best at refuting,
and Yìng Shào (應劭) was the foremost.
During the Jìn (晉) dynasty, Fù Xián (傅咸) was the best at deliberation,
and Fù Xián (傅咸) was the master.
However, Zhòng Yuán (仲瑗) was knowledgeable in ancient matters,
and arranged his arguments with sequence;
Cháng Yú (長虞) understood governance,
but his rhetoric was verbose.
And Lù Jī's (陸機) decisive arguments
also had sharp points,
but he did not cut out florid language,
somewhat burdening the essence of his writing.
Each had their own merits,
and their styles remain.
To begin with planning and deliberation,
to clearly use investigation to resolve doubts,
is how to respectfully and cautiously handle group affairs,
and to relax and tighten the reins of governance.
Therefore, what is relied upon in the general scheme
must pivot on the classics,
collect past examples from previous dynasties,
and observe the general changes in the present day.
The reasoning does not erroneously shake the branches,
and the words do not recklessly spread their splendor.
Moreover, suburban sacrifices must be deeply versed in ritual,
military affairs must be trained in warfare,
cultivating grains must first understand agriculture,
and judging lawsuits must be skilled in law.
Then, mark them with clear meaning,
summarize them with correct language,
make eloquence concise and pure,
and do not consider complexity and intricacy as skill;
make affairs clear and thorough,
and do not consider depth and obscurity as extraordinary.
These are the great essentials of the principles.
If one does not understand the system of governance,
but dances with the brush and plays with words,
separating and constructing phrases,
digging deep and fitting them together cleverly,
emptily displaying their splendor,
they will surely be rejected by the facts;
even if they obtain the reason,
it will also be buried by rambling words.
In the past, when the daughter of Qín (秦) married Jìn (晉),
those who followed as concubines wore embroidered clothing;
the people of Jìn (晉) valued the concubines and despised the daughter.
When the pearls of Chǔ (楚) were sold in Zhèng (鄭),
they were placed in cases made of scented cinnamon;
the people of Zhèng (鄭) bought the cases and returned the pearls.
If the writing floats above the reasoning,
and the peripheral surpasses the essential,
then the daughter of Qín (秦) and the pearls of Chǔ (楚)
will recur here.
Furthermore, "duì cè" (對策, responding with strategies)
means responding to an imperial decree and presenting policies.
"Shè cè" (射策, drawing lots for strategies)
means exploring affairs and offering proposals.
When the words hit the standard of reasoning,
it is like hitting the bullseye when shooting at a target.
Although the two names are different,
they are different forms of deliberation.
The ancient method of creating scholars
involved selecting based on affairs and examining their words.
In the middle years of Hàn Wén (漢文, Emperor Wen of Han),
the practice of recommending the virtuous and good began.
Cháo Cuò's (晁錯) response with strategies
became the head of the recommendation.
And when Xiào Wǔ (孝武, Emperor Wu) became even more enlightened,
he sought out outstanding talents,
those who responded with strategies were promoted to office as the first priority,
and those who drew lots for strategies entered officialdom with a first-class ranking.
This was truly an essential method for selecting the virtuous.
Looking at Cháo's (晁) response,
examining the past and clarifying the present,
his words were precise and clear,
and his affairs were comprehensive and sufficient.
He was promoted to a high rank,
which is certainly proof.
Dǒng Zhòngshū's (董仲舒) response
followed and narrated the *Chūnqiū* (春秋, Spring and Autumn Annals),
based on the transformations of Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽),
and investigated the changes of past dynasties;
his verbosity without confusion
was because the affairs and reasoning were clear.
Gōngsūn's (公孫) response
was simple and not extensive,
but he summarized the essentials with concise writing,
the matters were relevant and the emotions were expressed,
so the Tài Cháng (太常, Grand Master of Ceremonies) was placed below,
and the emperor promoted him above.
Dù Qīn's (杜欽) response
was brief and pointed to the matter,
and his words were used to proclaim governance,
and not created for writing's sake.
And later, Lǔ Pī (魯丕) of the Later Hàn dynasty,
whose language and tone were simple and plain,
passed the strategies with Confucian elegance,
and entered the highest rank alone.
All of these five families
are clear models from previous dynasties.
Since the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties,
they have gradually focused on literary beauty.
Using literature to record reality
has resulted in much being lost.
And when it came time for them to be selected,
they claimed illness and did not attend.
Even if one wanted to seek literature,
it could not be obtained.
Therefore, in the Hàn dynasty, the doctors were drinking
and pheasants gathered in the hall;
in the Jìn dynasty, the outstanding talents were tested
and deer gathered in front of them.
There is no other wonder,
the difference lies in the loss of selection.
Furthermore, refuting deliberation is biased and argumentative,
with each holding different views.
Responding with strategies is praising and promoting,
greatly illuminating the way of governance.
It makes affairs deep in political skills,
and reasoning dense in current affairs.
It weighs the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to forge the world,
and is not a lofty discussion that is slow and weak.
It controls changes in power to save customs,
and is not a harsh and insincere argument.
Its influence is vast and far-reaching,
and its flow is abundant without overflowing.
This is the beautiful response of the royal court.
How difficult it is
for a scholar to be talented!
Some are skilled in governance but lack literary talent,
and some are skilled in literature but lack governance.
Those selected by responding with strategies
are truly all-round talents,
whose ambition is sufficient and literature is far-reaching.
Are they not rare?
Therefore, Wèi Wén (魏文) said, "Literature values *qì* above all,
*qì*'s clarity or turbidity has a form,
it cannot be forced or obtained through effort."
Thus, in his evaluation of Kǒng Róng (孔融),
he said, "His *tǐ qì* is lofty and wondrous";
in his evaluation of Xú Gàn (徐幹),
he said, "At times he possesses the *qì* of Qí (齊)";
in his evaluation of Liú Zhēn (劉楨),
he said, "He possesses an untrammeled *qì*."
Gōng Gàn (公幹) also said:
"Kǒng (孔) is outstanding and remarkable,
truly containing an extraordinary *qì*;
the essence of his writing
is virtually unsurpassable."
All of these emphasize the importance of *qì*.
Pheasants and painted birds possess vibrant colors yet can only flutter a hundred paces;
they are fleshy but lack strength.
Hawks and falcons lack brilliant hues, yet their wings soar to the heavens;
their bones are strong and their *qì* is fierce.
Literary talent and ability
are similar to this.
If wind and bone lack color,
then fierce birds will gather in the writing world;
if color lacks wind and bone,
then pheasants will hide in literary gardens.
Only when adorned with brilliance and soaring high
is literature the *míng fèng* (鳴鳳, calling phoenix).
